summary: Defines three kinds of syndicated web feeds that publish entries across one or more documents: paged feeds, archived feeds that allow reconstruction of contents, and complete feeds. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A news feed split into pages or saved in a back-issue pile, so you can read it all.

questions: what is an archived atom feed
subtitle: Three ways to spread a syndicated web feed over several documents: paged, archived and complete.

tldr.problem: Syndicated feeds are often split into several documents to save bandwidth or give sliding-window access, but there was no standard way to say how the pieces fit together or whether a client can rebuild the whole feed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines complete feeds (one document holds everything, marked with fh:complete), paged feeds (documents tied together with first, last, previous and next links) and archived feeds (a subscription document plus stable archive documents tied together with prev-archive and next-archive links).
tldr.outcome: Clients know which kind of feed they are reading and what they can safely assume. Only archived feeds let a client reconstruct every entry without loss. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5005 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the specification for feed paging and archiving.

sections.title: Why Feeds Span Several Documents
sections.content:
Syndicated web feeds, in formats such as Atom, are often split into multiple documents to save bandwidth, allow "sliding window" access, or for other purposes. RFC 5005 formalizes two types of feeds that can span one or more documents, paged and archived feeds, and adds complete feeds for the case where a single document explicitly holds all entries.

Each type has its own trade-offs. Complete feeds are useful when a client does not need to remember previously seen entries. Paged feeds split entries among temporary documents and suit entries that are not long-lived. Archived feeds split entries among permanent documents and suit long-lived entries where clients must see every one. The meaning of a feed that combines these types is undefined.

Atom is the normative format (RFC 4287), but the mechanisms can be used with similar formats. Appendix B shows RSS 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: A big pile of news can be kept as one sheet, as flip-through pages, or as numbered back issues. Each choice suits a different job.

sections.title: Feed Documents and Logical Feeds
sections.content:
The RFC separates two ideas. A feed document is an Atom feed document or similar file; it may hold any number of entries and may or may not show the whole picture. A logical feed is the complete set of entries associated with a feed. The head section is the feed-wide metadata, such as the child elements of atom:feed.

The pieces of a multi-document feed are connected with Atom link relations. Relative URIs in those relations must be made absolute, as described in Section 5.1 of RFC 3986. The RFC uses the namespace prefix fh for http://purl.org/syndication/history/1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: One page of a comic is not the whole comic. The single page is the document, and the whole story is the logical feed.

sections.title: Complete Feeds
sections.content:
A complete feed is one document that contains all entries of the logical feed. Any entry not in the document SHOULD NOT be considered part of that feed. The RFC's example is a ranking that changes over time, such as "Top Twenty Records" or "Most Popular Items": newer entries should not be displayed next to older ones, and marking the feed as complete makes old entries get discarded on refresh.

A publisher marks a complete feed by putting the empty element fh:complete in the head section. The RFC defines no content for it and does not address duplicate entries in complete feeds.
sections.plainLanguage: A top-twenty chart is replaced each week. A complete feed tells readers to throw away last week's chart and keep only this one.

sections.title: Paged Feeds
sections.content:
A paged feed is a set of linked feed documents that together hold the entries of a logical feed, with no guarantee that each document's contents stay stable. Paged feeds are lossy: entries may be added or changed while a client walks through the pages, and the client may never notice. Clients SHOULD NOT present a paged feed as coherent or complete.

They suit feeds whose number of entries is very large, infinite or indeterminate. The RFC's example is a search engine publishing query results as pages, so large result sets do not overwhelm the server, network or client.

Four link relations tie the pages together: first (the furthest preceding document), last (the furthest following document), previous (the immediately preceding document) and next (the immediately following document). A paged feed document MUST have at least one of them and should carry as many as practical. Duplicate entries are not addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Paged feeds are like search result pages. The list can change while you flip through it, so you should not assume you saw everything.

sections.title: Archived Feeds
sections.content:
An archived feed is a set of feed documents that can be combined to accurately reconstruct the entries of a logical feed, without losing entries. This works through one subscription document, which always holds the most recently added or changed entries, and potentially many archive documents, which hold less recent entries. The entries in an archive document at a given URI SHOULD NOT change, and neither should its URI.

Three link relations connect them: prev-archive (the immediately preceding archive), next-archive (the immediately following archive) and current (the feed document with the most recent entries). Subscription and archive documents MUST have prev-archive unless no preceding archives exist. Archive documents SHOULD also have next-archive unless none follows, SHOULD point to their subscription document with current, and SHOULD contain the empty element fh:archive in the head section.

In the RFC's example the archives are monthly. The subscription document points to the 2003/11 archive, which points to 2003/10, and so on. The 2003/11 archive has no next-archive, because it is the latest complete archive; another one (2003/12) may be under construction, but linking to it before completion would be an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Archived feeds are like a magazine: this month's issue on the newsstand, and every older issue in a stack, each pointing to the one before it. Old issues never change, so you can collect them all.

sections.title: Publishing and Consuming Archives
sections.content:
Because archives are stable, a client that has fetched one can assume it will not meaningfully change, so a later edit may go unnoticed. A publisher who needs a change seen by everyone (for example a factual correction) should consider republishing the entry in the subscription document, in addition to or instead of the archive. Unimportant edits such as spelling fixes might be made only in archives. Publishers SHOULD build their feeds so duplicate removal is unambiguous, and they need not serve every archive; they may refuse (for example with HTTP 403 or 410) or be unable to serve it (404).

A client typically subscribes by polling the subscription document. If a prev-archive URI has not been processed before, it fetches that archive, adds the entries, and repeats until it reaches an archive it already processed, a missing prev-archive (the end of the archive) or an error.

When duplicates appear, clients SHOULD keep only the most recently updated entry; on a tie or without timestamps, the entry from the most recently updated feed document replaces the others. In Atom, entries are duplicates if they share the same atom:id, and update times come from atom:updated. Clients SHOULD warn users when they cannot rebuild the whole logical feed.
sections.plainLanguage: To catch up, you grab each missing back issue, going backwards until you reach one you already have. If two copies of a story exist, keep the newest. If an issue is missing, say so.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
These feeds have the same security considerations as Atom. Encryption and authentication can come from signing or encrypting the feed, or from channel mechanisms such as TLS and HTTP authentication, or IPsec transport. The RFC does not define what it means if different component documents of one logical feed use different security mechanisms.

The main new risk is denial of service: a crafted feed could make a client send excessive, or even endless, network requests. Clients can require user intervention after some number of requests or limit requests by a hard limit or heuristics; servers can deny requests they consider abusive. Clients should also watch resource limits when storing documents.

IANA added two link relations to the Link Relations registry, prev-archive and next-archive, and the previous, next and current relations should be updated to refer to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A tricky feed could keep sending you to the next page forever. A sensible reader stops after a while and a sensible server can say no.

sections.title: Use in RSS 2.0
sections.content: Appendix B is informative and shows the same ideas in RSS 2.0. There, two entries are duplicates if they have the same guid element. RSS 2.0 does not define an entry update time, but the feed-level update time can be taken from lastBuildDate if present. The RSS examples use the fh elements as well, and Atom link relations through atom:link, for a complete feed, a paged feed, a subscription document and an archive document.
sections.plainLanguage: The same labels work on a different kind of newsletter, so the idea is not tied to one format.
